title: A Recipe to Stop AI from Going Rogue - Nautilus
gist: George Washington University physicists Neil Johnson and Frank Yingjie Huo published a formula in Patterns claiming AI chatbots have an identifiable internal 'tipping point' before going rogue, located by where concepts sit on the model's learned semantic map, and that this point can be nudged.

insights.claim: Neil Johnson and Frank Yingjie Huo of George Washington University argue there is a visible tipping point embedded in an AI chatbot's internal workings when it goes off the rails, such as encouraging self-harm, spreading medical misinformation or supporting violent views.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: A predictable failure threshold would be valuable for AI safety tooling, liability management and regulation.
insights.quote: Johnson and Huo argue that there is a visible “tipping point” embedded in the internal code of an AI chatbot when it goes off the rails

insights.claim: According to Johnson and Huo, where a chatbot's tipping point lies depends on where certain concepts are stored on the model's semantic map, and that tipping point can be nudged.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Implies a potential intervention lever for model providers to reduce harmful outputs.
insights.quote: Where this tipping point lies depends on where certain concepts are stored on the giant semantic map within the AI agent’s network, and it can be nudged.

insights.claim: An AI model's semantic map is not designed by anyone; it emerges during training and places similar ideas close together and unrelated ideas far apart.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Safety properties emerge from training rather than explicit design, complicating guarantees.

insights.claim: The researchers' formula aims to prevent large language models from doing things that endanger humans, and was published in the peer-reviewed journal Patterns.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Academic physics-of-complex-systems approaches are entering the AI safety field.

insights.claim: The question of what makes an AI chatbot go rogue had become a pressing one in the weeks before October 2026.
